Ibn al-Qayyim's Commentary (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on Surah 37, verses 1–4:

Allah swears by His angels who line up (al-Saffat) in devotion before Him, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said to his Companions: "Will you not line up as the angels line up before their Lord?"

Complete the first rows and close ranks within the row, just as they (the angels) said of themselves: ﴿And indeed, we are those who line up (al-Saffun)﴾.

The "al-Saffat" are the angels whose wings are spread in the air. The "az-Zajirat" (those who drive) are the angels who drive the clouds and other things by the command of Allah. The "fat-Taliyat" (those who recite) are those who recite the speech of Allah.

It was also said that "al-Saffat" refers to birds, as Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Have they not seen the birds above them, spreading and folding their wings?﴾ and He says: ﴿And the birds in ranks﴾.

"Az-Zajirat" refers to the verses and the words that restrain from the disobedience of Allah, and "at-Taliyat" refers to those who gather the Book of Allah the Exalted.

It was also said that "al-Saffat" refers to fighting in His cause, "az-Zajirat" refers to the horses charging against His enemies, and "at-Taliyat" refers to those who remember Him at the encounter with their enemy.

It was also said that "al-Saffat" refers to those who gather and whose bodies line up in prayer, "az-Zajirat" refers to their souls restraining them from the disobedience of Allah, and "at-Taliyat" refers to His verses.

The wording admits all of this, though the most entitled to be included and the most fitting are the angels, for the oath serves as evidence, and the sign confirms what He swore to, namely monotheism. What is mentioned other than the angels is among the effects of the angels and comes through them.

By this oath Allah swore to the Oneness of His Lordship and His Divinity, and He established the Oneness of His Lordship by saying: ﴿Indeed, your God is One, Lord of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them, and Lord of the easts.﴾

This is one of the greatest proofs that He is the one God; for if there were another god with Him, that god would share with Him in Lordship just as he shared with Him in Divinity. Exalted is Allah far above that by a great exaltation. This is the method of the Qur'an: it establishes the Oneness of Divinity through the Oneness of Lordship, so it establishes that He alone is to be worshipped by establishing that He alone is the Creator and Provider. He specifically mentioned "the easts" here either because they indicate the "wests," since each of the two correlatives implies the other, or because the easts are the places where the stars rise and the sources of light, or as a preface to what follows of the adornment of the heaven with the ornament of the stars and their being a protection from every devil. Mentioning the easts is more fitting and suitable to this meaning. And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 37, verses 6–7:**

He adorned its lower heaven with the stars, and guarded it from the devils.

(Section)

Then reflect upon the wisdom of Allah, blessed and exalted, in these stars, their abundance, and the wondrous nature of their creation: that they are an adornment for the heaven and guides by which people are led in the paths of the land and the sea. He placed in them light and radiance such that we can see them despite their extreme distance. Were it not so, we would not be guided, would not have direction, and would not know the times. Then reflect upon how He subjected them, obedient to the command of their Lord, blessed and exalted, moving in one fixed course, which His wisdom and knowledge required that they not depart from. Among them He made the zodiacal constellations (al-buruj), the lunar stations (al-manazil), the fixed stars (al-thawabit), and the wandering planets (al-sayyarah); the large and the small, the medium, the bright white, and the reddish white.

Among them are some that are hidden from the observer so that he does not perceive them.

He divided the zodiac belt (mintaqat al-buruj) into two parts, elevated and lowered, and determined their movement as a single measure, and He set the sun, the moon, and the planets in their stations.

Among them is that which traverses it in one month, namely the moon.

Among them is that which traverses it in a year, and among them is that which traverses it in several years. All of this necessitates wisdom and providential care. He made these a means for what He, glory be to Him, brings about in this world, so that people may infer from them the events that coincide with them, just as they know what occurs with the rising of the Pleiades (al-Thurayya) when it rises, and its setting when it falls, among the events that accompany it. Likewise with the other stations and planets.

Then reflect upon His, glory be to Him, making the Great Bear (banat na'sh) and what is near it visible and never setting, because of their nearness to the pole (al-markaz), and because of the divine wisdom in that, and that they are like the signposts by which people are guided on unknown roads on land and sea. They look to them, and to the Pole Star (al-Jadi) and the two Guards (al-Farqadan) at every time they wish, and so they are guided wherever they will.

((Subtle point))

(The third heart) A heart filled with faith, illumined by the light of faith, from which the veils of desires have been lifted and those darknesses have departed. Its light within the breast radiates, and from that radiance there is a kindling such that if whisperings (waswas) came near it, they would be burned by it. It is like the sky which is guarded with stars: if Satan approaches it, he is pelted with them and burned.

The sky is not more sacred than the believer, and God's protection of him is more complete than the protection of the sky. The sky is the place of worship of the angels and the abode of revelation, and in it are the lights of acts of obedience; the heart of the believer is the abode of monotheism, love, knowledge and faith, and in it are their lights. So he is worthy to be guarded and protected from the enemy's plotting, so that it does not obtain anything from him except that it is snatched away.

He illustrated this with a fine example, namely three houses: a house belonging to a king, in which are his treasures, his stores and his jewels;

a house belonging to a servant, in which are the servant's treasures and stores, but not the king's jewels and stores;

and an empty house, bare, with nothing in it.

A thief came to steal from one of these houses. From which of them will he steal?

If you say from the empty house, it would be impossible, because the empty house has nothing in it to be stolen. For this reason it was said to Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: "The Jews claim that they do not have whisperings in their prayer." He said: "What can Satan do with a ruined heart?"

If you say he steals from the king's house, that would be like the impossible and the unattainable, for it has around it guards and watchmen and what the thief cannot approach. How (could he), when its guard is the king himself?

And how could the thief approach it when around it are the guards and soldiers that surround it?

So nothing remains for the thief except the third house, and it is the one he raids.

Let the discerning person contemplate this example with thorough contemplation, and let him apply it to the hearts, for they are upon its pattern.

As for a heart emptied of all good, which is the heart of the disbeliever and the hypocrite, that is the house of Satan, which he has secured for himself, settled in, and taken as a dwelling and a place of rest. So what is there for him to steal, when in it are his treasures, his stores, his doubts, his imaginings and his whisperings?

And a heart that has been filled with the majesty of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, His greatness, His love, His watchfulness over it, and modesty before Him: which Satan would dare to approach this heart? And if he wishes to steal something from it, what would he steal? His utmost is that he may, at times, seize a snatch and a plunder, obtaining it through a moment of heedlessness on the servant's part and a lapse that is inevitable, since he is a human being, and the rules of humanity apply to him: heedlessness, forgetfulness, distraction, and the dominance of natural disposition.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 37, verses 62–64:

Allah the Exalted said concerning the tree of zaqqum: ﴿Indeed, We made it a trial for the wrongdoers.﴾ [al-Saffat: 63].

Qatadah said: When Allah the Exalted mentioned this tree, the wrongdoers were tested by it, and they said: "Will there be a tree in the Fire, when the Fire consumes trees?"

So Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿Indeed, it is a tree that emerges from the root of Hellfire.﴾ [al-Saffat: 64].

Thus He informed them that its nourishment is from the Fire, meaning it is nourished by the Fire.

Ibn Qutaybah said: The tree of zaqqum may be a plant made of fire, and of a substance that the fire does not consume. Likewise are the chains of the Fire, its shackles, its fetters, its scorpions and its serpents. Had they been as we know them, they would not have survived the Fire. Allah the Exalted has only pointed us to what is unseen to Him by means of what is seen to us. So the names agree in their indication while the meanings differ, and what is in Paradise of its fruit, its furnishings, its trees and all its implements is of the same kind.

The purpose is this: this tree is a trial for them in this world, through their denial of it, and a trial for them in the Hereafter, through their eating from it.

And Allah the Exalted said concerning Noah, peace be upon him: ﴿And We left for him among later generations: "Peace be upon Noah among the worlds. Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good."﴾

And Allah the Exalted said concerning Abraham, His friend (khalil): ﴿And We left for him among later generations: "Peace be upon Abraham."﴾ [al-Saffat: 108-109]

And Allah the Exalted said concerning Moses and Aaron: ﴿And We left for both of them among later generations: "Peace be upon Moses and Aaron."﴾ [al-Saffat: 119-120]

And Allah the Exalted said: ﴿"Peace be upon the family of Yasin."﴾ [al-Saffat: 130] So what He left for His messengers among later generations is the peace upon them that was mentioned.

A group of the exegetes, among them Mujahid and others, said: "And We left for them among later generations" means the good praise and the truthful tongue (lisan al-sidq) for all the prophets. This is also the view of Qatadah. It is not proper to relate this as two opinions of the exegetes, as one who relates opinions does, but rather they are one view. Whoever says that what is left is the peace upon them among later generations itself, there is no doubt that His saying "Peace be upon Noah" is a clause in a position of accusative (nasb) governed by "We left," and the meaning is that the worlds greet Noah with peace and those after him among the prophets.

Whoever explains it as the truthful tongue and good praise has looked at the necessary consequence and effect of peace, which is praising them and the truthful tongue that Allah placed for them, on account of which they are greeted with peace whenever they are mentioned.

Ibn 'Atiyyah and others claimed that whoever says "We left for him" means good praise and a truthful tongue, then "Peace be upon Noah among the worlds" [is an independent sentence (jumlah ibtida'iyyah) having no place in i'rab, and it is peace from Allah by which He greeted him. They said: this peace from Allah is a safeguard for Noah among the worlds, that no one should mention him with evil. This was stated by al-Tabari.

This view is strengthened by the fact that He, the Exalted, informed that what was left for him is among later generations, and that the peace upon him is among the worlds, and by Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, saying: "Allah preserved for him good praise."

But this view is weak, for several reasons.

First: it necessitates omitting the object of "We left," and the speech would have no benefit remaining under this estimation. The meaning would reduce to "We left for him among later generations something without any mention of it in the wording," because for this speaker the peace is cut off from what precedes it and has no connection to the verb.

Second: if the object were omitted as they claim, it would have been mentioned in one place to show what is intended by its omission, and it would not be consistent across all the places where it is said that He left for them good praise. This is not the method of the Qur'an. Rather, it is eloquent to mention a thing in one place and omit it in another, since the mentioned indicates the omitted. Most of the time you find it mentioned and its omission is rare.

As for omitting something consistently, without mentioning it in any place, and with nothing in the wording indicating it, this does not occur in the Qur'an.

Third: in the reading of Ibn Mas'ud, ﴿And We left for him among later generations﴾ has "salaman" (peace) in the accusative (nasb). This indicates that what was left is the peace itself.

Fourth: if the peace were cut off from what precedes it, that would harm the eloquence and strength of the speech, and it would not be good to stop at what precedes it. Consider this from the state of the listener: when he hears His saying "And We left for him among later generations," how does his heart become eager and longing for the completion of the speech and for gathering its benefit? He does not find the benefit of the speech complete so that he may be satisfied with it, but remains seeking its completion, and that which is left. So stopping at "al-akhirin" is not a complete stop.

If it is said: the object may be omitted in this pattern, because "tarak" here means "a'ta" (gave), since He gave him good praise, which He left for him among later generations, and in the pattern of "a'ta" both objects may be mentioned, omitted, or one of them alone may be stated, and this occurs in the Qur'an. Such as His saying ﴿Indeed, We have given you al-Kawthar﴾, where both are mentioned.

And He said ﴿As for he who gives﴾, where both are omitted.

And He said ﴿And your Lord will surely give you﴾, where the second is omitted and the first is kept.

And He said ﴿who give zakah﴾, where the first is omitted and the second is kept. It is said: the verb "give" (i'ta') is a verb of praise, so its wording indicates that the object given has received the gift of the giver, and giving is kindness, benefit and goodness. Thus it is permissible to mention both objects, omit both, or keep one of them, according to the purpose intended by the verb. If the intent is to establish the reality of giving, which removes the servant from miserliness, stinginess and withholding that contradicts kindness, the verb is mentioned alone, as Allah the Exalted said ﴿As for he who gives and fears Allah﴾, without mentioning what is given or to whom. One says: so-and-so gives, gives charity, bestows, and does good.

The Prophet ﷺ said: "O Allah, there is none who can withhold what You give, and none who can give what You withhold." Since the intent here is the singling out of the Lord, the Exalted, in giving and withholding, mentioning the recipient has no meaning, nor does regard for the recipient. The intent is that the reality of giving and withholding belongs to You, not to another, and You alone possess it; none shares it with You. So mentioning the two objects here would harm the completeness of the meaning and its eloquence. And when the intent is to mention both together, as in His saying ﴿Indeed, We have given you al-Kawthar﴾ [al-Kawthar: 1], the purpose is to inform His Messenger ﷺ of what He singled him out with and gave him of al-Kawthar, and this is not complete without mentioning both objects. Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 37, verses 86–87:

Then, by God, what is the opinion of the people of major sins and the wrongdoers about God when they meet Him, and the wrongs done to people are with them?

If their saying would benefit them, "We have held good opinion of You, for You will not punish a wrongdoer or a corrupt person," then let the servant do whatever he wishes, and let him commit everything God has forbidden him, and let him think well of God, for the Fire will not touch him. So glory be to God! How far does delusion (ghurur) carry the servant? Indeed Abraham said to his people: ﴿Is it a falsehood, gods other than God that you desire? So what is your opinion of the Lord of the worlds?﴾ [al-Saffat: 86–87].

That is, what is your opinion of what He will do with you when you meet Him, having worshipped other than Him?

Whoever reflects on this passage with true reflection will know that good opinion of God is itself good action, for the servant is only moved to good action by his opinion of his Lord, that He will reward him for his deeds, recompense him for them, and accept them from him. So what moved him to action is good opinion; whenever his opinion is good, his action is good. Otherwise, good opinion combined with following desire is incapacity (ajz), as in the hadith of al-Tirmidhi and the Musnad from the narration of Shaddad ibn Aws, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "The shrewd one is he who holds himself accountable and works for what comes after death, and the incapable one is he who follows his desires and wishes (tamanna) from God."

In sum, good opinion only exists alongside the establishment of the causes of salvation; but alongside the establishment of the causes of destruction, good opinion cannot be realized.

The difference between good opinion (husn al-zann) and delusion (ghurur).

If it is said: Rather, that can be realized, and the basis of good opinion is the vastness of God's forgiveness, His mercy, His pardon and His generosity, and that His mercy precedes His wrath, and that punishment does not benefit Him, nor does pardon harm Him.

It is said: The matter is so, and God is above that and is more exalted, more noble, more generous and more merciful. But that is placed in its proper place which befits it, for He, glory be to Him, is described by wisdom, might, retribution, severity of seizure, and punishment of whoever deserves punishment. So if the reliance of good opinion were upon the bare attributes and names alone, the righteous and the wicked, the believer and the disbeliever, His ally and His enemy would all share in it. The names and attributes of God do not benefit the criminal when he has returned with His wrath and anger, has exposed himself to His curse, has fallen into what He forbade, and has violated His sanctities. Rather, good opinion benefits whoever repents, regrets, and gives up sin, replaces an evil deed with a good one, and faces the rest of his life with goodness and obedience, and then thinks well of God. This is good opinion; the former is delusion. And God is the One sought for help.

Do not skip this section, for the need for it is intense for everyone who distinguishes between good opinion of God and delusion regarding Him. God the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, those who believed, and those who emigrated and struggled in the way of God, those hope for the mercy of God, and God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 218]. So He made these the people of hope, not the idle and the corrupt.

He the Exalted said: ﴿Then indeed your Lord, for those who emigrated after they were tested, then struggled and were patient, indeed your Lord after these is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Nahl: 110]. So He informed, glory be to Him, that after these things He is Forgiving and Merciful to whoever does them. The scholar places hope in its proper places, while the ignorant deceived person places it in other than its proper places.

God the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, those who believed, and those who emigrated and struggled in the way of God, those hope for the mercy of God, and God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ [al-Baqarah: 218]. Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 37, verses 95–96 (part 1 of 2):

The words of the Most High: ﴿And Allah created you and what you do﴾

Many people have thought that (mā) in the Most High's words ﴿And Allah created you and what you do﴾ is a verbal noun (maṣdariyyah, i.e. the "mā" that turns the following verb into a verbal noun). They have used it as proof that human actions are created.

But it is not a verbal noun; rather it is a relative pronoun (mawṣūlah, meaning "that which").

The meaning is: "And Allah created you and the thing you do and carve of idols. So how can you worship it when it is created by Allah?"

Had it been a verbal noun, the statement would be more favourable as an argument for them than against them, since the meaning would be: "Do you worship what you carve, while Allah created your worship of it?" What meaning would there be in this, and what proof against them would it be?

The point is that each of the two often enters upon the other, and the sentence admits both equally.

(Section)

Abu al-Qasim al-Suhayli said: Know that when mā is a relative pronoun joined to a verb whose root is "to work," "to make," or "to do," and that action is attributed to an agent other than the Creator, glorified is He, it is not valid for it to refer to anything except a verbal noun, by the consensus of rational people among mankind in the Jahiliyyah and in Islam, that human actions do not attach to substances and bodies. You do not say "I made a camel," "I made a mountain," "iron," "a stone," or "dust." When you say "What I did pleased me" or "What Zayd did," you mean the act.

Accordingly, in interpreting the Most High's words ﴿And Allah created you and what you do﴾ there is no valid reading except the view of the People of the Sunnah, that the meaning is "And Allah created you and your actions." The view of the Mu'tazilah is valid neither by transmitted evidence nor by reason, for they claimed that mā refers to the stones they carved into idols, and said that the sense of the sentence is "created you and the idols which you make," out of their denial that our actions are created by Allah, glorified is He. They argued that the structure of the sentence requires what they said, because the Most High's earlier words are ﴿He said: Do you worship what you carve?﴾, so mā refers to the carved stones. This is valid neither grammatically nor in meaning.

As for grammar, it has already been established that mā cannot be a verbal noun with a specific verb.

As for meaning, they did not worship carving; they worshipped the carved objects. Since this is established, the verse, which is a refutation of them and a limitation upon them, must refer to the carved stones and the worshipped idols, and the sense would be: "You worship carved stones, while Allah created you and those stones which you make."

All of this is the meaning of the Mu'tazilah's view and the explanation of what they compared it to.

The arrangement of the verse according to the interpretation of the people of truth is more elegant and the argument more decisive. What they went to is corrupt and impossible, because they agreed with us that human actions do not fall upon substances and bodies.

If it is said: You say "I made the page" and "I made the bowl," and likewise bodies are made in this sense?

We reply: In what you mention, the verb attaches only to the form which is the assembling and composition, and that is the very act itself. As for the composed substance, it is not made by us. So the making and doing return to the acts, not to the substances. This is agreement between us and them, so it is not right to turn them away from that.

As for their claim of the beauty of arrangement and the inimitability of the speech, it is evident, and our interpretation is absent from theirs, because the verse came to show that the Creator deserves worship by His sole creation, and to establish proof against those who worship what does not create while they themselves create. So He said: ﴿Do you worship what you carve?﴾, that is, what does not create anything while you create, and you call for the worship of Him who created you and your actions which you do. Had the creation of actions not been attributed to Him in the verse, and had He attributed it to them by metaphor, the argument from the sentence itself would not have stood, because it would make them creators of their actions while He is creator of other kinds, and would thus make them His partners in creation.

Exalted is Allah above the saying of the deviators, and far from the stumbling of the falsifiers. How weak is their argument, how feeble the foundations of their doctrine, and how clear is the truth to whoever follows it. May Allah make us among its followers and its party.

What we have mentioned was said by Abu 'Ubayd regarding the saying of Hudhayfah concerning "that the craftsman's creation of the body and its making," and he cited the verse. Al-Qutaybi disagreed with him in correcting the error, and committed a more serious error, and he agreed with the Mu'tazilah in its interpretation even though he did not say their saying.

This is the end of the words of Abu al-Qasim.

He went to great lengths in rejecting what the verse cannot bear other than it, or what is more fitting to bear it and more suitable for it.

We, and every person of truth, agree that Allah is the Creator of the servants and their actions, and that every movement in the universe is created by Allah. The soundness of this doctrine is supported by more than a thousand proofs from the Noble Qur'an, the Sunnah, reason and the natural disposition. But the verse should not be carried to other than its appropriate meaning out of eagerness to make it an argument against them, for there is sufficiency in the other proofs without it.

Moreover, it is an argument against them from another aspect, together with mā meaning "that which," which we will explain, God willing.

Our discussion of the verse, God willing, is in two stations: first, the negation of its indication for the view of the Qadariyyah; and second, the affirmation of its indication for the view of the people of truth, contrary to their claim. So there are two stations: a station of affirmation and a station of negation.

As for the station of negation, the Qadariyyah claimed that the verse is an argument for them that they are creators of their actions. They said: Because Allah, glorified is He, attributed the actions to them, and this indicates that they are the originators of them. The intended meaning here is not the actions themselves but the carved idols. So He informed that He created them and created those idols which they made, and the intended meaning is their material, which is what the creation fell upon. As for their form, by which they became idols, it is by their actions, and He attributed that to them, so it is by their origination and creation.

This is the way they argue from the verse.

Some of those who affirm predestination and that Allah is the Creator of the actions of the servants opposed them, saying: The verse is explicit that their actions are created by Allah, for mā here is a verbal noun, and the meaning is "Allah created them and created their actions," and they established this with what al-Suhayli and others mentioned.

When the Qadariyyah objected to them: how can mā be a verbal noun here, and what way remains for arguing against them if the meaning is "Allah created you and your worship"? Is this anything other than teaching them an argument, by saying: "If Allah created our worship of the idols, then it is willed by Him; how then does He forbid us from it? And if it is created, how can we abandon it?" Is it permissible to argue against their worship in this way?

The affirmers replied: If you reflect upon the context of the verse and its purpose, you would know the soundness of the argument. For Allah, glorified is He, denied them the worship of one who creates nothing at all, and left the worship of the One who is the Creator of their essences and their actions. So if Allah is your Creator and the Creator of your actions, how can you call to His worship, and worship what creates nothing, neither your essences nor your actions?!

This is among the finest arguments. The denial of their worship of what does not create anything, and His equating it with the Creator, is repeated in the Qur'an, as in His words: ﴿Is He who creates like He who does not create? Will you not remember?﴾ and His words: ﴿Those whom they call upon besides Allah create nothing, while they are created﴾ and His words: ﴿This is the creation of Allah, so show me what those besides Him have created﴾,

and similar to these.

So the argument is sound, and the proof of the creation of actions together with the creation of essences is established. This is the furthest extent of the advance of the two groups in the verse, as you see.

The correct view is that it is a relative pronoun, and that it does not indicate the soundness of the Qadariyyah's position; rather it is an argument against them even though it is a relative pronoun. This is shown by a premise we mention before entering into the explanation: that the method of argument and address is to focus attention upon the matter for which and against which one argues. When the one arguing is refuting a claim that he has made about something while it contradicts that, he focuses attention upon showing the falsity of that claim, and that what the claim attributes to it is the opposite of its real state, not its real state. He cannot then leave that aside and mention the attribute of something else.

Given this, Allah, glorified is He, denied them their worship of idols and showed that they do not deserve worship. The context did not place in opposition to them the abandonment of His worship; rather what is in opposition is the worship of one who does not deserve worship. Had He said: "Do you not worship Allah while He created you and what you do?", the verbal-noun reading would have been definite, and it would not be fitting for it to mean "that which," since the meaning would be: "How do you not worship Him, when He is the One who brought you into being and brought your actions into being? He is the Benefactor to you with both kinds of bringing into being and creation."

This is the parallel of what they established about its being a verbal noun.

As for the context of the verse, it is in the position of denying their worship of one who does not deserve worship. So it must show a meaning that contradicts his being worshipped. This meaning is shown by his being a created thing, and whoever is created by Allah, one of His creatures, should not be worshipped, and worship is not fitting for him.

Consider the agreement of this meaning with His words: ﴿Those whom they call upon besides Allah create nothing, while they are created﴾, how He denied them the worship of gods that are created by Him, glorified is He, and that do not create. This clarifies the meaning of His words: ﴿And Allah created you and what you do﴾.

Its parallel is His words in Surat al-A'raf: ﴿Indeed, those you call upon besides Allah are servants like you﴾, that is, they are created servants as you are, so how can you worship what is created?

Consider the method of the Qur'an. Had He intended the meaning they mention, of His good attributes and His sole creation, as in the saying of the man of Ya-Sin: ﴿And why should I not worship He who originated me?﴾

Here, since the purpose was to inform them of the goodness of His worship and His deserving it, He mentioned the reason for that, which is that He is the Creator of His worshipper and the Originator of him. This is a blessing from Him upon him, so how could he abandon His worship? Had this been the intended meaning of His words: ﴿And Allah created you and what you do﴾, it would have required that it be said: "Will you not worship Allah while He is the Creator of them and the Creator of their actions?"

Reflect upon it, for it is clear.

As for Abu al-Qasim's statement in establishing the Mu'tazilah's argument from the verse, that it is not valid for it to be a verbal noun, this is false grammatically, and it is not so.

As for his claim that mā does not occur as a verbal noun with a specific verb, its falsity has already been shown, for its verbal-noun use does occur with a specific but indefinite verb, as in the Most High's words: ﴿For what they broke of their covenant with Allah and what they had promised Him, and for what they used to lie﴾, and His words: ﴿while you recite the Book﴾, and His words: ﴿That is for what you used to exult in the land without right, and for what you used to behave insolently﴾, and to many times that number. All these are specific verbs, and they are more specific than the general notion of action. So if it comes as a verbal noun with these verbs, its coming as a verbal noun with the general "action" is more fitting.

Their saying that they did not worship carving but worshipped the carved object is a corrupt argument, for the discussion concerns mā accompanying the verb, not mā accompanying the verb of carving. The first cannot bear anything other than the relative pronoun, and it does not follow from the second being a verbal noun that the first is too.

So this is a corrupt formulation.

As for his arguing that it is also a verbal noun by what he mentioned, there is no proof for him in it.

As for his statement: "The actions of the servants do not fall upon substances and bodies," it may be asked: what is the meaning of their not falling upon substances and bodies?

Do you mean that their actions do not attach to bringing them into being? Or do you mean that they do not attach to changing and shaping them? Or do you mean something more general than that? Or is it what is common to both divisions?

If you mean the first, it is granted, but it benefits you nothing, for the fact that it is a relative pronoun does not entail that. The idols being made by them does not require that their material be made by them, but it is like their saying: "I made a house, I made a door, I made a wall, I made a garment."

This is a true usage, established rationally, linguistically, by the Law and by custom, and no objection can reach it. So this is the same as the idols being made.

If you mean that their actions do not attach to shaping them, that is certainly false.

If you mean the common element, that too is false, for it contains the negation of a truth together with a falsehood. The negation of the falsehood is correct, but the negation of the truth is false.

Then it is said: the act of making upon substances and bodies may be expressed with the specific verb, and its witness in the verse is "Do you worship what you carve?" Here mā is a relative pronoun, so their act, which is carving, has fallen upon the body. In that case, what difference is there between their specific actions falling upon the substance and body, and their general actions falling upon it? Not in the sense that its essence is made by them, but in the sense that their act is what made it an idol and made it deserve the name of idol, just as by their making it became carved and deserved this name. This is clear.

As for his statement, in answering the objection with "I made the page and I made the bowl," that the verb attaches to the form which is assembling and composition, and that is the act itself, then likewise it attaches to the shaping by which the stone became a carved idol. The two are equal.

As for his statement that the verse is in explanation of the Creator's deserving worship by His sole creation, its answer has already been given, and that the verse came to explain that their deities do not deserve worship because they are created by Allah, and we have mentioned its witnesses from the Qur'an.

If it is said: it would have sufficed to say: "Do you worship what you carve, while Allah created it?" So when He turned to His words: ﴿And Allah created you and what you do﴾, it is known that He intended to argue against them concerning abandoning His worship, glorified is He, while He is their Creator and the Creator of their actions?

It is replied: In mentioning His creation of their gods and of those who worship them, there is in it a disclosure of the ugliness of their state and the corruption of their opinion and intellects in worshipping them rather than Him, Exalted, which is not present in merely mentioning the creation of the gods alone. For when Allah, Exalted, is the One who created you and created the deities you worship, they are created like you. How then does a sane person worship one who is like himself, deify him, and single him out with the utmost reverence, glorification and love?!

Is this anything but the most abominable injustice against yourselves and against your Lord? Exalted is He has indicated this meaning in His words: ﴿Indeed, those you call upon besides Allah are servants like you﴾.

It is among the rights of the worshipped that he not be like the worshipper, for if he is like him, he is a created servant. The one worshipped should be a Lord and Creator.

This is among the finest and clearest of arguments. The intended meaning from the context has become clear to you in its sound form, its explanation has been made plain to you, and by the praise of Allah the difficulty has been removed. The veil of ambiguity has been lifted from the meaning, and it has become evident that Ibn Qutaybah was successful in his explanation of the verse, just as he was successful in agreeing with the People of the Sunnah regarding the creation of the servants' actions.

Do not find this section lengthy, for it will establish for you principles which you can hardly hear in the course of lectures, and it will yield for you rules and foundations which you will not find in most books.

If it is said: Where is what you promised of deriving proof from the verse for Allah's creation of the servants' actions, on the assumption that mā is a relative pronoun?

It is replied: Yes, the promise has already preceded, and the time for fulfilling it has come, and the time for presenting it has arrived. The way of deriving proof from it on this assumption is that Allah, glorified is He, informed that He created them and created the idols which they made, and those idols only became idols by their actions. So that name does not fall upon them except after their making. If He, glorified is He, is the Creator, then the soundness of this application requires that He is the Creator of it entirely, meaning its material and its form. When its form is created by Allah just as its material is, it follows that He is the Creator of their very action by which the form came about, because it arises from their own movements. When Allah is the Creator of it, their actions which give rise to what is created by Allah are created by Him. This is a better and more subtle argument than making mā a verbal noun. Its parallel as an argument is the same, in His words: ﴿And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring in the laden ship, and We created for them of its likeness that which they ride﴾.

The more correct view is that the created likeness here is the ships, and He informed that they are created, and they only became ships by the actions of the servants. Whoever said that the likeness here is the land ships, which are camels, is further from the truth, for two reasons:

First: they are not called a likeness to ships, neither linguistically nor in reality, for two likes are that one of them fills the place of the other. The reality of likeness is that it be between one ship and another ship, not between a camel and a ship.

Second: His words following it, ﴿And if We will, We drown them, and there is no one to cry for them﴾, are an indication that the intended meaning is the ships, which when they ride them, We are able to drown them. So He reminded them of His blessings upon them in two respects: first, their riding them; and second, that He keeps them safe from drowning when they ride them.

A parallel argument of the same kind is His Most High words: ﴿And Allah has made for you, from what He created, shades, and He has made for you refuges in the mountains, and He has made for you garments that protect you from the heat and garments that protect you from your violence﴾.

The garments they wear are made for them, and He has informed that He is the One who made them, and they only became garments by their actions.

Its parallel is: ﴿And Allah has made for you, from your houses, a place of rest, and He has made for you, from the skins of livestock, houses﴾ [al-Nahl 16:80].

The houses that are made from the skins of livestock are the tents, and they became houses through their work.

If you say: Is what is meant by all of this the material and not the form?

I say: The material does not deserve these names by which people have applied them. Rather, these names are deserved only after it has been worked and its forms have come to subsist in it. He has informed that these things are created for Him in this state, and Allah knows best.

Here, since the purpose was to inform them of the goodness of His worship and His deserving it, He mentioned the reason for that, which is that He is the Creator of His worshipper and the Originator of him. This is a blessing from Him upon him, so how could he abandon His worship? Had this been the intended meaning of His words: ﴿And Allah created you and what you do﴾, it would have required that it be said: "Will you not worship Allah while He is the Creator of them and the Creator of their actions?"

Reflect upon it, for it is clear.

As for Abu al-Qasim's statement in establishing the Mu'tazilah's argument from the verse, that it is not valid for it to be a verbal noun, this is false grammatically, and it is not so.

As for his claim that mā does not occur as a verbal noun with a specific verb, its falsity has already been shown, for its verbal-noun use does occur with a specific but indefinite verb, as in the Most High's words: ﴿For what they broke of their covenant with Allah and what they had promised Him, and for what they used to lie﴾, and His words: ﴿while you recite the Book﴾, and His words: ﴿That is for what you used to exult in the land without right, and for what you used to behave insolently﴾, and to many times that number. All these are specific verbs, and they are more specific than the general notion of action. So if it comes as a verbal noun with these verbs, its coming as a verbal noun with the general "action" is more fitting.

Their saying that they did not worship carving but worshipped the carved object is a corrupt argument, for the discussion concerns mā accompanying the verb, not mā accompanying the verb of carving. The first cannot bear anything other than the relative pronoun, and it does not follow from the second being a verbal noun that the first is too.

So this is a corrupt formulation.

As for his arguing that it is also a verbal noun by what he mentioned, there is no proof for him in it.

As for his statement: "The actions of the servants do not fall upon substances and bodies," it may be asked: what is the meaning of their not falling upon substances and bodies?

Do you mean that their actions do not attach to bringing them into being? Or do you mean that they do not attach to changing and shaping them? Or do you mean something more general than that? Or is it what is common to both divisions?

If you mean the first, it is granted, but it benefits you nothing, for the fact that it is a relative pronoun does not entail that. The idols being made by them does not require that their material be made by them, but it is like their saying: "I made a house, I made a door, I made a wall, I made a garment."

This is a true usage, established rationally, linguistically, by the Law and by custom, and no objection can reach it. So this is the same as the idols being made.

If you mean that their actions do not attach to shaping them, that is certainly false.

If you mean the common element, that too is false, for it contains the negation of a truth together with a falsehood. The negation of the falsehood is correct, but the negation of the truth is false.

Then it is said: the act of making upon substances and bodies may be expressed with the specific verb, and its witness in the verse is "Do you worship what you carve?" Here mā is a relative pronoun, so their act, which is carving, has fallen upon the body. In that case, what difference is there between their specific actions falling upon the substance and body, and their general actions falling upon it? Not in the sense that its essence is made by them, but in the sense that their act is what made it an idol and made it deserve the name of idol, just as by their making it became carved and deserved this name. This is clear.

As for his statement, in answering the objection with "I made the page and I made the bowl," that the verb attaches to the form which is assembling and composition, and that is the act itself, then likewise it attaches to the shaping by which the stone became a carved idol. The two are equal.

As for his statement that the verse is in explanation of the Creator's deserving worship by His sole creation, its answer has already been given, and that the verse came to explain that their deities do not deserve worship because they are created by Allah, and we have mentioned its witnesses from the Qur'an.

If it is said: it would have sufficed to say: "Do you worship what you carve, while Allah created it?" So when He turned to His words: ﴿And Allah created you and what you do﴾, it is known that He intended to argue against them concerning abandoning His worship, glorified is He, while He is their Creator and the Creator of their actions?

It is replied: In mentioning His creation of their gods and of those who worship them, there is in it a disclosure of the ugliness of their state and the corruption of their opinion and intellects in worshipping them rather than Him, Exalted, which is not present in merely mentioning the creation of the gods alone. For when Allah, Exalted, is the One who created you and created the deities you worship, they are created like you. How then does a sane person worship one who is like himself, deify him, and single him out with the utmost reverence, glorification and love?!

Is this anything but the most abominable injustice against yourselves and against your Lord? Exalted is He has indicated this meaning in His words: ﴿Indeed, those you call upon besides Allah are servants like you﴾.

It is among the rights of the worshipped that he not be like the worshipper, for if he is like him, he is a created servant. The one worshipped should be a Lord and Creator.

This is among the finest and clearest of arguments. The intended meaning from the context has become clear to you in its sound form, its explanation has been made plain to you, and by the praise of Allah the difficulty has been removed. The veil of ambiguity has been lifted from the meaning, and it has become evident that Ibn Qutaybah was successful in his explanation of the verse, just as he was successful in agreeing with the People of the Sunnah regarding the creation of the servants' actions.

Do not find this section lengthy, for it will establish for you principles which you can hardly hear in the course of lectures, and it will yield for you rules and foundations which you will not find in most books.

If it is said: Where is what you promised of deriving proof from the verse for Allah's creation of the servants' actions, on the assumption that mā is a relative pronoun?

It is replied: Yes, the promise has already preceded, and the time for fulfilling it has come, and the time for presenting it has arrived. The way of deriving proof from it on this assumption is that Allah, glorified is He, informed that He created them and created the idols which they made, and those idols only became idols by their actions. So that name does not fall upon them except after their making. If He, glorified is He, is the Creator, then the soundness of this application requires that He is the Creator of it entirely, meaning its material and its form. When its form is created by Allah just as its material is, it follows that He is the Creator of their very action by which the form came about, because it arises from their own movements. When Allah is the Creator of it, their actions which give rise to what is created by Allah are created by Him. This is a better and more subtle argument than making mā a verbal noun. Its parallel as an argument is the same, in His words: ﴿And a sign for them is that We carried their offspring in the laden ship, and We created for them of its likeness that which they ride﴾.

The more correct view is that the created likeness here is the ships, and He informed that they are created, and they only became ships by the actions of the servants. Whoever said that the likeness here is the land ships, which are camels, is further from the truth, for two reasons:

First: they are not called a likeness to ships, neither linguistically nor in reality, for two likes are that one of them fills the place of the other. The reality of likeness is that it be between one ship and another ship, not between a camel and a ship.

Second: His words following it, ﴿And if We will, We drown them, and there is no one to cry for them﴾, are an indication that the intended meaning is the ships, which when they ride them, We are able to drown them. So He reminded them of His blessings upon them in two respects: first, their riding them; and second, that He keeps them safe from drowning when they ride them.

A parallel argument of the same kind is His Most High words: ﴿And Allah has made for you, from what He created, shades, and He has made for you refuges in the mountains, and He has made for you garments that protect you from the heat and garments that protect you from your violence﴾.

The garments they wear are made for them, and He has informed that He is the One who made them, and they only became garments by their actions.

Its parallel is: ﴿And Allah has made for you, from your houses, a place of rest, and He has made for you, from the skins of livestock, houses﴾ [al-Nahl 16:80].

The houses that are made from the skins of livestock are the tents, and they became houses through their work.

If you say: Is what is meant by all of this the material and not the form?

I say: The material does not deserve these names by which people have applied them. Rather, these names are deserved only after it has been worked and its forms have come to subsist in it. He has informed that these things are created for Him in this state, and Allah knows best.

(Lataifa: on the station of khullah)

It is a station that admits no rivalry from anything other than the Beloved. The taking of a child is a branch among the branches of the heart. The Beloved was jealous over His intimate friend, lest there dwell in a branch of his heart something other than Him. So He commanded him to slaughter him. When he submitted in compliance, that rivalry departed and love was purified for its rightful owner. Then the glad tidings came: ﴿And We ransomed him with a tremendous sacrifice﴾.

The intent was not that he should be punished, but that he should be tested so as to be refined.

The wonder is not in the Friend's command to slaughter the son; the wonder is in his carrying out the slaughter with his own hand. Had it not been for total immersion in love of the command, such a command would not have been easy to bear. Therefore its traces were made a place of return for hearts, which yearn for them more intensely than birds yearn for their nests.

(Chapter)

Consider the state of our third father, Ibrahim, the imam of the upright ones (hunafa'), the shaykh of the prophets, the pillar of the world, and the Friend of the Lord of the worlds among the children of Adam.

Consider what his trial led to, his patience, and his giving of himself to God.

Consider how his giving of himself to God and his support of His religion led to God taking him as a khalil for Himself, and commanding His Messenger and Friend Muhammad (ﷺ) to follow his creed. I will point out to you one quality of the many things God honoured him with in his trial of slaughtering his son. God, blessed and exalted, rewarded him for surrendering his son to God's command by blessing his offspring and multiplying them until they filled the plain and the mountain. God, blessed and exalted, is not outdone in generosity by anyone, and He is the most generous of the generous.

Whoever leaves something for His sake, or does something for His sake, God gives him multiples of what he left of that thing, many times over, and rewards him with many times over what he did for His sake. When Ibrahim was commanded to slaughter his son, he hastened to obey God's command, and the son agreed with his father, out of mutual contentment and submission. God, knowing their truthfulness and fidelity, ransomed him with a tremendous sacrifice and gave them what He gave them of His bounty. Among some of His gifts was that He blessed their descendants until they filled the earth, for the purpose of having children is nothing but procreation and the multiplication of offspring. For this reason Ibrahim said: ﴿My Lord, grant me [a child] from the righteous﴾, and said: ﴿My Lord, make me an establisher of prayer, and [also] from my descendants﴾.

The utmost of what he feared and dreaded from slaughtering his son was the cutting off of his line. When he gave his son to God, and the son gave himself, God multiplied his offspring for him, blessed them, and increased them until they filled the world, and He placed prophethood and the Book among his descendants exclusively, and brought forth from them Muhammad. It is mentioned that Dawud (peace be upon him) wished to know the number of the Children of Israel, so he commanded that they be brought together, and sent for that nuqaba' (leaders) and 'urafa' (overseers), and ordered them to report the count to him. They remained for a period unable to accomplish that. Then God revealed to Dawud: "You know that I promised your father Ibrahim, when he was commanded to slaughter his son and hastened to obey My command, that I would bless his descendants until they become equal to the stars. Make them such that their number cannot be counted. You wish to count a number that I have decreed cannot be counted." He mentioned the rest of the hadith. Thus He made from his line these two great nations whose number none can count but God, their Creator and Provider: the Children of Israel and the Children of Isma'il. Apart from this, God honoured him with the elevation of his mention and beautiful praise, on the tongues of all nations, and among the angels in the heavens. This is part of the fruit of his dealing with God. So woe to the one who knows Him and then deals with others: how losing his bargain is, and how great his regret.

[Section: The Perfection of Love]

Then khullah includes the perfection and ultimate end of love, such that no room remains in the heart for anything other than the beloved. It is a station that does not accept sharing in any way. This station is specific to the two Friends, may the prayers and peace of God be upon them both: Ibrahim and Muhammad, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "God has taken me as a khalil just as He took Ibrahim as a khalil."

In the Sahih, from him (ﷺ), he said: "If I were to take a khalil from among the people of the earth, I would have taken Abu Bakr as a khalil, but your companion is the khalil of God."

In another hadith: "I disavow before every khalil his khullah."

When Ibrahim (peace be upon him) asked for a child and was given one, and his love was attached to his heart, a branch was taken from it. The Beloved was jealous over His khalil that there should be a place in his heart for another, so He commanded him to slaughter him. The command was in a dream, so that carrying out the command would be a greater trial and test. The intent was not the slaughter of the child, but the slaughter of him from the heart, so that the heart would be purified for the Lord. When the Friend (peace be upon him) hastened to comply and placed the love of God above the love of his son, the aim was achieved, the slaughter was lifted, and he was ransomed with a tremendous sacrifice. For the Lord, exalted, never commanded something and then utterly annulled it; rather, He must leave some part of it or a substitute for it, just as He left the law of ransom, and just as He left the recommendation of charity before private conversation, and just as He left the five prayers after the fifty were removed and kept their reward, saying: "The word is not changed before Me: they are five in action and fifty in reward."

[Section: Love and Khullah]

As for what some of the confused think, that love is more perfect than khullah, and that Ibrahim is the khalil of God while Muhammad is the beloved of God, this is from their ignorance. For love is general and khullah is specific, and khullah is the ultimate end of love. The Prophet (ﷺ) informed that God took him as a khalil just as He took Ibrahim as a khalil, and he denied that he could have a khalil other than his Lord, while he informed of his love for Aisha, her father, Umar ibn al-Khattab, and others.

Also, God, glorified is He, says: ﴿Indeed, God loves those who are constantly repentant and loves those who purify themselves﴾ [al-Baqarah: 222]. And ﴿God loves the patient﴾ [Aal 'Imran: 146]. And ﴿God loves the doers of good﴾ [Aal 'Imran: 148]. And ﴿God loves those who act justly﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 42]. The young repentant one is a beloved of God, but khullah is specific to the two Friends. This is only from a lack of knowledge and understanding of God and His Messenger (ﷺ).

(Chapter)

Khullah is the love that penetrates the spirit and heart of the lover until no place remains in it for anything other than the beloved, as it has been said:

"You have penetrated the path of the spirit within me, and for this the intimate friend was named khalil."

This is the secret for which—and God knows best—the Friend was commanded to slaughter his son, the fruit of his heart and the morsel of his liver. For when he asked for a son and was given one, a branch of his heart became attached to him. Khullah is a station that does not accept partnership or division. So the Friend was jealous over his khalil that there should be a place in his heart for another. He therefore commanded him to slaughter the son, to remove the rival from his heart.

When he prepared himself for that and resolved upon it with a firm resolve, the purpose of the command was achieved. There was no benefit left in taking the son's life, so He prevented it and ransomed him with a tremendous sacrifice. He was told: ﴿O Ibrahim, you have fulfilled the vision﴾ [al-Saffat: 104], that is, you acted as one who affirms it. ﴿Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good﴾ [al-Saffat: 80], We reward whoever hastens to obey Us, so We gladden his eye just as We gladdened your eye by your compliance with Our commands, and by preserving the son and his safety. ﴿Indeed, this was the clear trial﴾ [al-Saffat: 106]: it is the Beloved's testing of His lover, and His examining him so that he prefers His pleasure. Thus He perfects His blessings upon him; it is a trial of affliction and a gift of grace upon him together.

This call, to which only the special ones of His creation are summoned, and among them the people of intellect and insight, is not answered by everyone. Not every eye is comforted by it. Its people are those who are in the midst of the right hand's grasp on the day of the two graspings, and the rest of the people of the right hand are at its edges.

"Not every eye is comforted by the Beloved, nor does everyone who is called answer the caller."

"Whoever does not answer the caller of your guidance, leave him; he will answer everyone who has become a caller to error."

"And say to the inflamed eyes: beware of seeing the light of the sun, so cover yourself against the darkness of the nights."

"And forgive souls that did not give themselves to their beloved; leave them and what they chose, and do not be harsh."

[Section: The Drowning]

The Shaykh al-Islam said:

(Chapter of Drowning) God Most High said: ﴿So when they had both submitted and he put him down upon his forehead﴾ [al-Saffat: 103].

This is a term by which, in this chapter, is indicated one who has reached the middle of the station and passed the limit of separation.

The manner of his inference from the indication of the verse: when Ibrahim (ﷺ) and his son reached what they reached in hastening to comply and resolving to carry out the slaughter commanded, the father laid him upon his forehead at once, took the knife and swung it toward his throat. In that state he turned away from himself and his son, and passed away by God's command from them both. Thus he entered the sea of gathering of secret, heart, and concern upon God, and passed the limit of distinction that prevents compliance with this command.

His words: "﴿When they had both submitted﴾" means they surrendered and yielded to God's command, so there remained no dispute from either the father or the son, but pure submission and complete surrender.

His words: "﴿and he put him down upon his forehead﴾" means he threw him down upon his forehead, which is the side of the brow that faces the ground when one lies down, and that is the posture of one who is to be slaughtered.

His words: "he reached the middle of the station" he does not mean a specific station, and for this reason he left it indefinite and did not restrict it. The "station" among them is a stage of the stations of the wayfarers, and it differs according to its levels, and it has a beginning, a middle, and an end. The "drowning" referred to is to become in the middle of the station.

If it is said: drowning is more specific to the end of the station than to its middle, because it is immersion in it, such that it engulfs the heart and concern, so how does the Shaykh make it a middle in it?

I say: when the seeker's aspiration in this state is gathered upon the aim, and he turns away from all else, he has departed from the station of distinction and passed its limit into the station of gathering. He begins within the station, and the beginning of every station resembles the end of the one before it. When he reaches the middle of it, it engulfs his heart, concern, and will, just as one drowns who reaches the middle of a deep sea before arriving at its far shore.

(Section: That the Sacrifice Was Isma'il (peace be upon him))

Isma'il is the one who was sacrificed according to the correct view of the scholars among the Companions, the Successors, and those after them.

As for the claim that it was Ishaq, it is false for more than twenty reasons. I heard Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyya—may God sanctify his spirit—say: this view is only taken from the People of the Book, and it is even false by the text of their own book. For in it: God commanded Ibrahim to slaughter his son, his firstborn, and in one wording: his only son. The People of the Book, along with the Muslims, do not doubt that Isma'il is his firstborn. What deceived the proponents of this view is that in the Torah in their hands is: "Slaughter your son Ishaq." He said: this addition is from their distortion and lying, for it contradicts His saying: "Slaughter your firstborn and your only one." But the Jews envied the sons of Isma'il this honour and wished it to be theirs, and to bring it to themselves and claim it for themselves apart from the Arabs. But God refuses except to make His favour belong to its people. How could it be said that the sacrificed one was Ishaq, when God gave glad tidings to Ishaq's mother of him and of his son Ya'qub? God Most High said, speaking of the angels, that they said to Ibrahim when they brought him the glad tidings: ﴿Do not fear, for we have been sent to the people of Lut.—And his wife was standing, and she laughed, and We gave her glad tidings of Ishaq, and after Ishaq, Ya'qub﴾ [Hud: 70–71]. It is impossible that He should give her the glad tidings that a child will be born to her and then command that he be slaughtered. And there is no doubt that Ya'qub (may God be pleased with him) is included in the glad tidings, so the glad tidings include Ishaq and Ya'qub in one wording, and this is the apparent meaning of the speech and its context.

If it is said: had the matter been as you have mentioned, "Ya'qub" would have been in the genitive as a conjunction with Ishaq, and the reading would be ﴿and after Ishaq, Ya'qub﴾, that is, "and Ya'qub from after Ishaq".

It is said: the nominative does not prevent Ya'qub from being the one given glad tidings, because glad tidings are a specific speech, and it is the first true joyful report.

God's words: ﴿and after Ishaq, Ya'qub﴾ [Hud: 71] is a sentence that includes these conditions, so it is glad tidings; indeed, the true reality of glad tidings is the declarative sentence.

And since glad tidings are speech, the position of this sentence is in the accusative by way of reporting after a verb of saying, as if the meaning is: "and We said to her: after Ishaq, Ya'qub." And the speaker, when he says, "I gave so-and-so glad tidings of the arrival of his brother and his family behind him," is understood by no one except as giving glad tidings of both matters together. This is what no person of understanding doubts at all. Then another matter weakens the genitive reading: the weakness of your saying, "I passed by Zayd and after him 'Amr," and because the conjunction stands in the place of the preposition, so it is not separated from the genitive, just as the preposition is not separated from the genitive.

Ibn al-Qayyim's commentary on Surah 37, verses 102–107 (part 2 of 2):

And it is also indicated by the fact that when Allah, glorified is He, mentioned the story of Ibrahim and his son, the one who was sacrificed, in Surah (al-Saffat), He said: ﴿So when they both had submitted, and he put him down upon his forehead, And We called to him, "O Ibrahim, You have fulfilled the vision." Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good. Indeed, this was the clear trial. And We ransomed him with a great sacrifice. And We left for him among later generations: "Peace upon Ibrahim." Thus do We reward the doers of good. Indeed, he was among Our believing servants.﴾ [al-Saffat: 103–111].

Then He said, exalted is He: ﴿And We gave him the good news of Ishaq, a prophet from among the righteous.﴾ [al-Saffat: 112]. This is a good news from Allah, exalted is He, to him, as a reward for his patience in what he was commanded. This is very clear that the one given the good news of was other than the first, rather it is almost explicit in that.

If it is said: The second good news was about his prophethood, meaning that when the father was patient in what he was commanded, and the son submitted to the command of Allah, Allah rewarded him for that by granting him prophethood.

It is said: The good news was given regarding the whole: his very person and existence, and that he would be a prophet. That is why "nabiyyan" is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal muqaddar), meaning: "destined to be a prophet." So it is not possible to take the good news as referring to the essence and then restrict it to a subordinate circumstantial clause that functions like an adjunct; this is an absurd way of speaking. Rather, when the good news concerns his prophethood, then its concerning his existence is more fitting and more appropriate.

Also, there is no doubt that the one sacrificed was in Makkah, which is why the sacrifices on the day of sacrifice (yawm al-nahr) are performed there, just as the sa'i between al-Safa and al-Marwa and the stoning of the pillars (rami al-jimar) were prescribed as a reminder of the matter of Isma'il and his mother, and to keep alive the remembrance of Allah. It is well known that Isma'il and his mother were the ones who were in Makkah, not Ishaq and his mother. For this reason, the place and time of the sacrifice are connected to the Sacred House (al-Bayt al-Haram), whose building was shared by Ibrahim and Isma'il, and slaughtering in Makkah was part of the completion of the Hajj to the House, which was established by the hand of Ibrahim and his son Isma'il, in time and place. Had the sacrifice been in al-Sham, as the People of the Book claim and those who took from them maintain, then the sacrifices and the slaughter would have been in al-Sham and not in Makkah.

Also, Allah, glorified is He, named the one sacrificed "Halim" (forbearing), because none is more forbearing than one who submits himself to slaughter in obedience to his Lord. And when He mentioned Ishaq, He named him "'Alim" (knowing). He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Has there come to you the story of the honored guests of Ibrahim? When they entered upon him and said, "Peace." He said, "Peace, a people unknown."﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 24–25]

Up to His saying: ﴿They said, "Do not fear," and gave him good tidings of a knowing boy.﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 28]

This is Ishaq without doubt, because he was from his wife, and she was the one who was given the good news of him. As for Isma'il, he was from the concubine (suriyyah). Also, both of them were given the good news of him in old age and despair of having a child, whereas Isma'il was born before that.

Also, Allah, glorified is He, established the human custom that the firstborn is more beloved to the parents than those born after him. When Ibrahim, peace be upon him, asked his Lord for a child and He granted him one, a portion of his heart became attached to love for him. And Allah, exalted is He, had taken him as a close friend (khalil), and friendship (khullah) is a station that requires the singling out of the Beloved with love, and that no one else be made to share in it. So when the son took a portion of the father's heart, the jealousy of the friendship came to pull it out of the heart of the Khalil. So He commanded him to sacrifice the beloved. When he proceeded to sacrifice him, and the love of Allah was greater in his heart than the love of the son, the friendship was then purified of any admixture of partnership. Thus there remained no benefit in the slaughter, since the benefit lay in the resolve and the settling of the soul upon it. The purpose had been achieved, so the command was abrogated, the sacrificial son was ransomed, the Khalil confirmed the vision, and the Lord's objective was fulfilled.

It is known that this trial and test occurred with the first-born only, and it would not have occurred with another child apart from the first. Rather, in the other child there was no competition with the friendship that would call for a command to slaughter him. This is most evident.

Also, Sarah, the wife of the Khalil (ﷺ), was extremely jealous of Hajar and her son, for she was a slave-girl. When she bore Isma'il and his father loved him, Sarah's jealousy intensified, so Allah, glorified is He, commanded that Hajar and her son be taken away from her and settled in the land of Makkah, so that the heat of jealousy would cool from Sarah. This was from His mercy and compassion, exalted is He. How then would He command, after this, that her son be slaughtered while the son of the slave-girl is left as he is? This is with Allah's mercy toward her, the removal of harm from her, and His restoring her. How then would He command, after this, the slaughter of her son rather than the son of the slave-girl? Rather, His perfect wisdom required that He command the slaughter of the son of the concubine, so that the heart of the mistress would soften toward her and her son, and the harshness of jealousy would turn into mercy, and the blessing of this slave-girl and her son would become manifest to her, and that Allah does not waste a household of which this woman and her son are part. And so that He might show His servants His restoring after breaking, His gentleness after hardship, and that the outcome of the patience of Hajar and her son in distance, loneliness, strangeness and submission to the slaughter of the son, led to what it led to: making their traces and footsteps rites for His believing servants and acts of worship for them until the Day of Resurrection. This is His sunnah, exalted is He, toward whomever He wills to elevate among His creation: that He bestows favor upon him after his weakness, humiliation and brokenness. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We wished to confer favor upon those who were oppressed in the land and make them leaders and make them the inheritors.﴾ [al-Qasas: 5]

That is the bounty of Allah, which He gives to whom He wills, and Allah is the possessor of great bounty.

(Section)

And he said in Ighathat al-Lahfan, quoting Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah in his book "al-Jawab al-Sahih liman Baddala Din al-Masih":

He said: In their Torah, Allah, glorified and exalted is He, said to Ibrahim, peace be upon him: "Sacrifice your son, your firstborn, your only one, Ishaq," an addition by them to the wording of the Torah.

I say: This is definitively false from ten aspects.

The first: his firstborn and only son is Isma'il, by the consensus of the three faiths. So combining that he was commanded to sacrifice his firstborn with specifying him as Ishaq is combining two contradictories.

The second: Allah, glorified and exalted is He, commanded Ibrahim to move Hajar and her son Isma'il away from Sarah and settle them in the wilderness of Makkah, lest Sarah be upset. So He commanded the removal of the concubine and her son from her, preserving her heart and averting the harm of jealousy from her. How then would He, glorified and exalted is He, after this command the slaughter of Sarah's son and leave the concubine's son? This is something wisdom does not require.

The third: the story of the sacrifice was certainly in Makkah, and for this reason Allah made the slaughter of offerings and sacrifices in Makkah, as a reminder to the community of what happened between their father Ibrahim and his son.

The fourth: Allah, glorified is He, gave Sarah, mother of Ishaq, the good news: ﴿of Ishaq, and after Ishaq, Ya'qub﴾ [Hud: 71]. So He gave her the good news of both together. How then would He, after that, command the slaughter of Ishaq, when He had given their parents the good news of the child of his child?

The fifth: when Allah, glorified and exalted is He, mentioned the story of the one sacrificed, and his surrender of himself to Allah, and Ibrahim's proceeding to sacrifice him, and finished his story, He said after it:
﴿And We gave him the good news of Ishaq, a prophet from among the righteous.﴾ [al-Saffat: 112].
So Allah gave thanks for his submission to His command and his offering of his son to Him, and made among his reward for that that He gave him Ishaq. Thus Isma'il was saved from the slaughter, and Ishaq was added to him.

The sixth: Ibrahim, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, asked his Lord for a child. Allah answered his supplication and gave him the good news, and when the boy reached the age of striving with him, He commanded him to sacrifice him. He said, exalted is He:
﴿And he said, "Indeed, I will go to my Lord; He will guide me. My Lord, grant me [a child] from among the righteous." So We gave him good tidings of a forbearing boy.﴾ [al-Saffat: 99–101].
This is evidence that this child was given the good news after his supplication and his asking his Lord to grant him a child, and this one given the good news of is certainly the one commanded to be sacrificed, by the explicit text of the Qur'an.

As for Ishaq, he was given the good news without any supplication from him, rather in old age, and when someone like him could not have a child, and the good news of him was given to his wife Sarah. For this reason she marvelled at the birth of a child from her and him.

He said, exalted is He: ﴿And our messengers did come to Ibrahim with good tidings. They said, "Peace." He said, "Peace," and he did not delay to bring a roasted calf. But when he saw their hands not reaching toward it, he regarded them with suspicion and felt from them fear. They said, "Fear not; indeed, we have been sent to the people of Lut." And his wife was standing, and she laughed, so We gave her good tidings of Ishaq and after Ishaq, Ya'qub. She said, "Oh, woe to me! Shall I give birth while I am an old woman and this, my husband, is an old man? Indeed, this is an amazing thing." They said, "Are you amazed at the command of Allah?"﴾

So reflect on the context of this good news and that, and you will find them to be two different good tidings, with different origins, one distinct from the other.

The first good news was to him. The second was to her.

The first good news is the one in which the one to be sacrificed was given the good news of, not the second.

The seventh: Ibrahim, peace be upon him, never brought Ishaq to Makkah at all, nor did he separate him from his mother. And how would Allah command him to take the son of his wife, to sacrifice him in the place of his co-wife in her land, and leave the son of his co-wife?

The eighth: when Allah took Ibrahim as a Khalil, friendship implies that his entire heart be attached to his Lord, with no portion of it left for another. When he asked for a child, He gave him Isma'il, and a portion of his heart became attached to him. So His Khalil, glorified is He, wanted that portion to be for Him alone, not for any other creature. So He tested him by commanding the slaughter of his son. When he proceeded to comply, that friendship was purified for Him, and became purely for Allah alone. So the command to slaughter was abrogated, since the purpose had been achieved, which was the resolve and the settling of the soul upon compliance.

It is known that this occurs with the firstborn, not with the last. When this purpose was achieved from the first child, there was no need for the same in the other child. For if the love of the other child had competed with the friendship, he would have been commanded to slaughter him as he commanded the first. And if the one commanded to be slaughtered had been the other child, then He would have permitted him, with the first, to compete with the friendship for a long period, and then commanded him to remove that competitor afterward. This contradicts the requirement of wisdom, so reflect on it.

The ninth: Ibrahim, peace be upon him, was granted Ishaq in old age, and granted Isma'il in his youth and vigor. It is customary that the heart is most attached to the firstborn children, and inclines to him most and loves him most, unlike one granted a child in old age. The position of a child after old age is like the position of desire for a woman.

The tenth: the Prophet, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, used to take pride in saying:
"I am the son of the two sacrificed ones."
meaning his father Abdullah, and his grandfather Isma'il.

(Lataifa: on the station of khullah)

It is a station that admits no rivalry from anything other than the Beloved. The taking of a child is a branch among the branches of the heart. The Beloved was jealous over His intimate friend, lest there dwell in a branch of his heart something other than Him. So He commanded him to slaughter him.
