Among them: He singled them out with His tawhid, His love, His nearness, and the particular closeness to Him, with what He did not single out any other household with.

Among them: He established them in the land, made them successors in it, and the people of the earth obeyed them in what did not occur for others.

Among them: He strengthened them, supported them, and granted them victory over His enemies and their enemies, with what He did not give to others.

Among them: He effaced through them the traces of the people of error and polytheism, and the traces that He hates and abhors, which He did not efface through anyone else.

Among them: He planted for them love, reverence, and exaltation in the hearts of the worlds, which He did not plant for others.

Among them: He made their traces on earth a cause for the survival and preservation of the world, so the world will remain as long as their traces remain; when their traces disappear from the earth, that is the time of the world's ruin.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Allah made the Kaaba, the Sacred House, a support for the people, and the Sacred Month, and the offerings and the garlands﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 97].

Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said in its explanation: "If all the people abandoned the Hajj, the sky would fall upon the earth."

And he said: "If all the people abandoned the Hajj, they would not be given respite."

At that time the ruin of the world will draw near. Whoever reflects upon the domination Allah the Exalted gives to those enemies He empowers over lands and servants will know that this is due to their neglect of the religion of their Prophet, his sunnahs, and his laws. So Allah empowers over them those who destroy them and take vengeance upon them, until the lands in which the traces, sunnah, and laws of the Messenger (ﷺ) become manifest are protected from it, according to the manifestation of that among them.

For this reason the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) commanded us to ask Allah the Exalted to bless him and his family just as He blessed this exalted House, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon them all.

Among the blessings of the people of this House is that Allah the Exalted manifested through their hands blessings of this world and the Hereafter that He did not manifest through the hands of the people of any other household; and among their blessings and distinctions is that Allah the Exalted gave them distinctions that He did not give to others.

Among them is one whom He took as a friend, and among them is the Sacrificed one, and among them is one to whom He spoke directly and brought near as a confidant; among them is one to whom He gave half of beauty and made him among the most honoured of people before Him; among them is one to whom He gave a kingdom that He gave to no one else; and among them is one whom He raised to a lofty station.

When the Exalted mentioned this House and its offspring, He informed that He preferred all of them over the worlds.

And among their distinctions and blessings upon the people of the earth is that Allah the Exalted lifted the general punishment from the people of the earth because of them and because of their being sent. It was His custom, the Exalted, with the nations of the prophets before them, that when they denied their prophets and messengers, He destroyed them with a punishment that encompassed them, as He did to the people of Noah, the people of Hud, the people of Salih, and the people of Lot. When Allah the Exalted sent down the Torah, the Gospel, and the Qur'an, He lifted by them the general punishment from the people of the earth, and commanded jihad against those who denied them and opposed them. This became a victory for them through their own hands, a healing for their hearts, the taking of martyrs from among them, and the destruction of their enemy by their hands, so that the beloved things of Allah the Exalted might be achieved through their hands. Among the rights of the people of this House, and some of their virtues, is that the tongues never cease to be moist with blessings and peace upon them, and with praise and exaltation, and that the hearts are filled with their reverence, love, and honour; and that the one who sends blessings upon them knows that even if he spent all his breaths in sending blessings upon them, he would not fulfil the least of their rights. May Allah reward them on behalf of His creation with the best of rewards, increase them in exaltation, honour, and dignity in the Highest Assembly, and send blessings upon them with a lasting blessing that has no end, and grant them complete peace.

This verse has two readings.

One of them is "Ilyasin" (إلياسين), on the pattern of "Ismail." It has two possible interpretations.

The first: it is a second name for the Prophet Ilyas (Elias), and "Yasin" is his other name, like "Mikal" and "Mikail" (Michael).

The second: it is a plural, and this has two possible interpretations.

The first: it is the plural of Ilyas, whose original form was "Ilyasin," with two yas, like "Ibraniyyin" (Hebrews). One of the two yas was dropped, so it became "Ilyasin," and what is meant is his followers, as Sibawayh related: "al-Ash'arun" and "mithluhu" and "al-A'jamun."

The second: it is the plural of Ilyas with the ya omitted.

The second reading is "salamun 'ala Il yasin" (سَلامٌ عَلى إلْ ياسِينَ), and it has several interpretations.

The first: "Yasin" is the name of his father, so "Al" is added to it, as one says "Al Ibrahim" (the family of Abraham).

The second: "Al Yasin" is Ilyas himself, so "Al" is an annexed term added to "Yasin," and what is meant by "Al" is Yasin himself, as the earlier scholars mentioned.

The third: it is by deleting the nisba ya, so it is said "Yasin," and its original form is "Yasiyin," as previously mentioned. Its "Al" means their followers in their religion.

The fourth: "Yasin" is the Qur'an, and its "Al" are the people of the Qur'an.

The fifth: it is the Prophet (ﷺ), and his "Al" are his relatives and followers, as will come later. All these opinions are weak.

What led their proponents to them is their difficulty with the annexation of "Al" to "Yasin," whose name is "Ilyas" and "Ilyasin," and they transmitted it in the Mushaf written separately. Some reciters read it as "Al-Yasin," and a group of them said: it has the names Yasin, Al-Yasin, and Ilyas.

Another group said: Yasin is the name of someone else.

Then they differed. Al-Kalbi said "Yasin" is Muhammad (ﷺ).

Another group said it is the Qur'an. All of this is clear artificiality for which there is no need.

The correct view, and Allah knows best, is that the original phrase is "Al Yasin," like "Al Ibrahim," so the alif and lam at its beginning were dropped because of the gathering of similar sounds, and because the name indicates the place of what was omitted. This is common in their speech: when similar sounds gather, they dislike pronouncing them all, so they drop from them what can be dropped without confusion, even though they do not drop it in a position where similar sounds do not gather. For this reason they drop the nun from "inni," "anni," "ka'anni," and "lakinni," but they do not drop it from "laytani." Since the lam in "la'alla" resembles the nun, they dropped the nun along with it, especially as the Arabs' habit with a foreign name is to change it, so they say at one time "Ilyasin," at another "Ilyas," at another "Yasin," and perhaps they say "Yas."

On one of the two readings, peace has been upon him, and on the other reading, peace has been upon his family.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 37, verse 146:

Yaqtin (yaqṭīn): it is the gourd (dubbāʾ) and the squash (qarʿ). Although yaqṭīn is a more general term, in the language it refers to every plant that does not stand upon a stalk (sāq), such as the watermelon, the cucumber, and the cucumber-like melon (khiyār). Allah Most High said: ﴿And We caused to grow over him a tree of gourd.﴾ [al-Saffat: 146].

If it is said: that which does not stand upon a stalk is called najm (a low-growing plant), not shajar (a tree), and shajar is that which has a stalk, as the lexicographers have said. How then did He say: ﴿a tree of gourd﴾?

The answer: when shajar is used without qualification, it refers to that which has a stalk on which it stands; but when it is qualified by something, it becomes restricted by that qualification. The distinction between the absolute and the restricted in nouns is an important and greatly beneficial topic for understanding and for the levels of the language.

The yaqṭīn mentioned in the Qur'an is the plant of the gourd, and its fruit is called dubbāʾ, qarʿ, and "the tree of yaqṭīn." It is established in the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from the hadith of Anas ibn Mālik: that a tailor invited the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to a meal he had prepared. Anas (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "I went with the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and he brought him bread made of barley and broth in which there was gourd and dried meat. Anas said: I saw the Messenger of Allah ﷺ seeking out the gourd from around the dish, and I have not ceased to love the gourd since that day."

Abū Ṭālūt said: "I entered upon Anas ibn Mālik (may Allah be pleased with him), and he was eating squash and saying: O you, what a tree you are, how beloved you are to me, because of the love of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ for you."

In al-Ghaylāniyyāt: from the hadith of Hishām ibn ʿUrwah, from his father, from ʿĀʾishah (may Allah be pleased with her), who said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said to me: "O ʿĀʾishah, when you cook a pot, add plenty of gourd to it, for it strengthens the heart of the sorrowful."

Yaqṭīn: it is cold and moist, providing little nourishment, and it passes through quickly. If it does not spoil before digestion, it produces a praiseworthy humour (khilṭ maḥmūd), and one of its properties is that it produces a praiseworthy humour that is similar to what accompanies it. If it is eaten with mustard, it produces a pungent humour; with salt, a salty humour; and with an astringent, an astringent one. If it is cooked with quince, it nourishes the body with excellent nourishment.

It is a subtle, watery substance that provides moist, phlegmatic nourishment. It benefits those with hot temperaments (maḥrūrīn), and does not suit those with cold temperaments (mabrūdīn), nor those in whom phlegm predominates. Its water quenches thirst and removes a hot headache when drunk or when the head is washed with it. It is laxative to the belly however it is used, and those of hot temperament do not treat themselves with its like, and nothing is quicker in benefit than it.

Among its benefits: when it is smeared with dough and baked in an oven or tandoor, and its water is extracted and drunk with some gentle drinks, it calms the heat of burning fever, quenches thirst, and nourishes well. When it is drunk with terengabin (a laxative resin) and preserved quince, it purges pure yellow bile.

When gourd is cooked and its water is drunk with some honey and some natron (naṭrūn, a mineral salt), it expels phlegm and bile together. When it is pounded and made into a poultice on the crown of the head (yāfūkh), it benefits hot inflammations of the brain.

When its gourd-pulp is pressed and its water is mixed with rose oil and dripped into the ear, it benefits hot inflammations; and its pulp is beneficial for hot inflammations of the eye, and for hot gout (niqris). It is very beneficial for people of hot temperaments and for those with fever. When it meets bad humour in the stomach, it is transformed into its own nature, and it spoils and produces a bad humour in the body; the harm of this is averted with vinegar and murrī (fermented fish sauce).

In summary, it is among the most subtle of foods, and the quickest to be affected. It is related from Anas (may Allah be pleased with him) that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to eat it abundantly.

(Fā'idah) — A benefit/note.

"Aw" (or) is placed to indicate one of the two things mentioned with it. For this reason it occurs in a report whose truth is in doubt, since doubt is a wavering between two matters without preference for either over the other. It is not that "aw" is placed to express doubt. It may occur in a report about which there is no doubt, when the matter is left vague to the addressee and the speaker does not intend to clarify it for him, as in the words of the Exalted: ﴿And [sent him] to a hundred thousand or they would exceed [that]﴾ (37:147).

That is, they were so numerous that it could be said of them, "They are a hundred thousand or more." So "aw" indicates one of two things: either a hundred thousand alone, or a hundred thousand with an addition. The one reporting in all of this is not in doubt.

As for His words: ﴿Then they are like stones or even harder in hardness﴾ (2:74), some have held in this context, as in His words ﴿or like a rain-cloud from the sky﴾ (2:19), that "aw" here is the "aw" of permissibility (ibahah), meaning that the addressees are permitted to liken them to this or to that. This is corrupt, for "aw" was never placed for permissibility in any utterance; rather it remains on its own basis.

As for His words ﴿or like a rain-cloud from the sky﴾, He, exalted is He, mentioned two parables struck for the hypocrites in two different states, so they cannot be free of one of the two states. Thus "aw" retains its basis of indicating one of the two meanings, just as you say: "Zayd cannot be free of being either in the mosque or in the house," where you mention "aw" because you intend one of the two things. Reflect on the verse in light of what precedes it, and understand its meaning, and you will find the matter as I have described to you. The meaning is not "We permit you to liken them to this or to that."

As for His words ﴿Then they are like stones or even harder in hardness﴾, He mentioned hearts and did not mention a single heart. So they are, in general, hard; or, specifically, they are not free of one of two matters: either they are like stones, or they are harder in hardness.

From this is the poet's saying:

"I said to them: two things are unavoidable for you — / the breasts of lances that have been aimed, or chains."

That is, both are unavoidable in general. Then he detailed the two: some of them face the lances, which kill, and some of them face the chains, which take captive.

So this is detailed and specific, while the former is general.

Thus both matters occur in general, and their detail is by what follows "aw."

It may be permissible in His words, exalted is He, ﴿or even harder in hardness﴾ to be like ﴿a hundred thousand or they would exceed [that]﴾.

As for "aw" which is for choice (takhyir), the matter in it is clear.

As for the "aw" they claim is for permissibility, as in "Sit with al-Hasan or Ibn Sirin":

Permissibility is not derived from the word "aw," nor from its meaning, and "aw" is never for permissibility. Rather, permissibility is taken from the imperative form, which is for permissibility. This is shown by the fact that those who say "aw" is for permissibility must also say it is for obligation when it occurs between two things one of which must be done, as in your saying to one who must expiate: "Feed ten needy persons or clothe them." Here the obligation does not derive from "aw" but from the imperative; likewise, "Sit with al-Hasan or Ibn Sirin."

Ibn al-Qayyim, *al-Tafsir al-Qayyim*, on Surah 37, verses 180–182:

He exalted Himself above what those who describe Him say, and He sent peace upon the messengers because what they described Him with was free from every deficiency and flaw. He praised Himself, for He is the One described with the attributes of perfection that make Him deserving of praise, and He is exalted above every deficiency that contradicts the perfection of His praiseworthiness.

(Section)

As for the twelfth question, which is: what is the wisdom in God's sending peace (salam) upon His prophets and messengers, given that salam is a request and a supplication, so how can it be conceived of from God?

This is a question of great importance that deserves attention and should not be neglected. Few grasp its secret, except one whom God has granted special understanding and care. This is not the concern of the people of this age, whose most accomplished in transmission can do no more than relate sayings and counter-sayings, and whose most accomplished in investigation can do no more than raise a possibility and display a difficulty.

As for the verification of knowledge as it should be:

> For wars there are men who stand ready to wage them,
> and for the registers there is a book and a reckoning.

It would have been better for us to hold back, to rein in the pen, to join them on their own field, and to address them in what they are familiar with. We should not unveil the brides of meanings before the blind, nor escort their maidens to the impotent. But this is a commodity and merchandise that has its own polish, a bride that has its own suitor. It will reach its people and be given to its husband. Let us not prolong the oration, for it is the outburst of one who is afflicted. Let us return to the matter at hand and say:

There is no doubt that a request (talab) involves three elements: a requester (ṭālib), a requested thing (maṭlūb), and one from whom it is requested (maṭlūb minhu). (Section)

As for the twelfth question, which is: what is the wisdom in God's sending peace (salam) upon His prophets and messengers, given that salam is a request and a supplication, so how can it be conceived of from God?

This is a question of great importance that deserves attention and should not be neglected. Few grasp its secret, except one whom God has granted special understanding and care. This is not the concern of the people of this age, whose most accomplished in transmission can do no more than relate sayings and counter-sayings, and whose most accomplished in investigation can do no more than raise a possibility and display a difficulty.

As for the verification of knowledge as it should be:

> For wars there are men who stand ready to wage them,
> and for the registers there is a book and a reckoning.

It would have been better for us to hold back, to rein in the pen, to join them on their own field, and to address them in what they are familiar with. We should not unveil the brides of meanings before the blind, nor escort their maidens to the impotent. But this is a commodity and merchandise that has its own polish, a bride that has its own suitor. It will reach its people and be given to its husband. Let us not prolong the oration, for it is the outburst of one who is afflicted. Let us return to the matter at hand and say:

There is no doubt that a request (talab) involves three elements: a requester (ṭālib), a requested thing (maṭlūb), and one from whom it is requested (maṭlūb minhu). Its reality is not established except by these three pillars. Their distinctness is evident when the requester asks something from another, as in the familiar request, such as one who commands or forbids another, or asks him a question. But when the requester asks from himself, the requester is then the one from whom it is requested, and there are only two elements: a requester and a requested thing, while the one from whom it is requested is the requester himself.

If it is said: How can it be conceived that the requester and the one from whom the request is made are one, when they are two distinct realities? Just as the requested thing and the one from whom it is requested cannot be unified, nor the requested thing and the requester, likewise the requester and the one from whom the request is made cannot be unified. How then can a person be conceived of as requesting from himself?

It is said: This is what caused the matter to be obscure and problematic, and it must be uncovered and explained. We say: The difference between will (irada) and request (talab) is that request belongs to the category of wills. The one who wills, when he wills from another that he do something, likewise wills from himself that he do it. The self-directed request, though not identical to will, is more specific than it, and will is like the genus for it. Just as it is conceivable that the one who wills wills from himself, so also he requests from himself. The distinction between request and will, and what has been said about it, belongs to another place than this. The point here is that a living being's request from himself is an intelligible matter that everyone knows from himself. Moreover, it is known that a person may command himself and forbid himself. God the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, the soul is a persistent commander of evil﴾

And He said: ﴿But as for one who feared the standing before his Lord and restrained the soul from desire﴾

And the poet said:

> Do not forbid a trait while committing its like;
> shame upon you, when you do it, is great.
>
> Begin with yourself and restrain it from its error,
> and when it desists from it, then you are wise.

This is more than its evidences can enumerate. If it is intelligible that a person commands and forbids himself, and command and prohibition are requests, even though above him there is one who commands and forbids, then how is it impossible for One above whom there is no commander or forbidder to request from Himself the doing of what He loves and the leaving of what He hates? When this is understood, one understands the secret of His, blessed and exalted is He, sending peace upon His prophets and messengers, and that it is a request He made from Himself for their safety. If your mind does not contain this, I will add further clarification: He, glory be to Him, has informed in His Book that He prescribed mercy upon Himself. This is an obligation He imposed upon Himself. He is the one who obligates and the object of the obligation which He imposed, so He obligated Himself by Himself. The Prophet (ﷺ) confirmed this meaning with what clarifies it fully and reveals its reality, in his saying in the authentic hadith: "When God decreed creation, He wrote in a Book with His hand, over Himself, which is deposited with Him above the Throne: Indeed My mercy overcomes My wrath." And in another wording: "Has preceded My wrath."

Narrated by al-Bukhari, Muslim and al-Tirmidhi.

So reflect: how He emphasized this request and obligation by mentioning the act of writing, the attribute of the hand, the place of writing, that it is a Book, and the mention of the Book's place, that it is with Him above the Throne. This is an obligation affirmed with several kinds of emphasis, and it is an obligation He imposed on Himself. Among this is His saying: ﴿And it was ever incumbent upon Us to help the believers﴾. This is a right He made binding upon Himself, so it is a request and an obligation upon Himself, expressed by the word "right" (ḥaqq) and the word "upon" ('alā). Among this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) to Mu'adh in the authentic hadith: "Do you know what God's right upon His servants is?" He said: "I said: God and His Messenger know best." He said: "Their right is that they worship Him and do not associate anything with Him. Do you know what the servants' right upon God is when they do that?" I said: "God and His Messenger know best." He said: "Their right upon Him is that He not punish them with the Fire."

Narrated by al-Bukhari and Muslim.

Among it is His saying (ﷺ) in other than this hadith: "Whoever does such and such, it is a right upon God that He does such and such to him." This is in the context of promise and threat.

This right is what He made binding upon Himself. Among it is the hadith in the Musnad from Abu Sa'id, from the Prophet (ﷺ), concerning the words of one walking to prayer: "I ask You by the right of this walking of mine, and by the right of those who ask You." So this is a right that those who ask have upon Him, which He made binding upon Himself. Not that they obligated it nor made it binding, but He made it binding upon Himself to answer whoever asks Him, just as He made it binding upon Himself in the hadith of Mu'adh not to punish those who worship Him. So the right of those who ask upon Him is that He answer them, and the right of those who worship Him is that He reward them. Both rights are what He made binding and obligatory, not the askers nor the worshippers, but He, glory be to Him.

> Nothing that the servants have upon Him is an obligatory right;
> every deed and effort is not lost before Him.
>
> If they are punished, it is by His justice; if they are blessed, it is by His bounty,
> for He is the Generous, the Vast.

Among it is His saying: ﴿A promise binding upon Him in truth, in the Torah, the Gospel, and the Qur'an﴾. This promise is the truth which He made binding upon Himself and obligated. A parallel to this is what He informed of by His oath that He would do such and such, such as: ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely question them all﴾ and His saying: ﴿So by your Lord, We will surely gather them and the devils﴾ and His saying: ﴿We will surely destroy the wrongdoers﴾ and His saying: ﴿He said, "The truth, and the truth I say: I will surely fill Hell with you and those among them who follow you, all together"﴾ and His saying: ﴿So those who emigrated, were expelled from their homes, were harmed in My cause, fought, and were killed, I will surely remove from them their misdeeds and admit them into gardens beneath which rivers flow﴾ and His saying: ﴿So We will surely question those to whom messengers were sent, and We will surely question the messengers﴾, and similar to these in what He informed He would do with an emphatic oath. An oath in such a case implies exhortation or prohibition, unlike an oath concerning what He has done, such as His saying: ﴿Ya, Sin. By the wise Qur'an, indeed you are among the messengers﴾

And an oath affirming what the deniers reject is an emphasis of the report, and it belongs to the category of oath that implies affirmation. This is why the jurists say: an oath is that which implies a right, or a prohibition, or affirmation, or denial. The oath that implies exhortation or prohibition belongs to the category of request, because exhortation and prohibition are requests. Among this is what He informed He must do because of the precedence of His word, such as His saying: ﴿And已 Our word has already preceded for Our servants, the messengers, that they would indeed be helped, and that Our army would indeed be the victorious﴾ and His saying: ﴿And the word of your Lord has been fulfilled: "I will surely fill Hell with jinn and men all together"﴾ and His saying: ﴿And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord﴾

So this is a report of what He does and leaves undone, that because of the precedence of His word it will not change. Among this is His, glory be to Him, prohibiting what He prohibited for Himself, such as His saying, related from His Messenger (ﷺ): "O My servants, I have forbidden injustice to Myself and made it prohibited among you, so do not wrong one another."

Narrated by Muslim and al-Tirmidhi.

This prohibition is parallel to that obligation, and one should not give heed to the false interpretations that have been offered about it. Whoever considers the context of these passages and their purpose will be certain that such interpretations are far from the intended meaning. Like the saying of some who claim that the meaning of writing and obligating in all of this is His informing of it, and the meaning of "your Lord has prescribed upon Himself mercy" is that He informed about it regarding Himself, and His saying "I have forbidden injustice to Myself" means "I have informed that it will not occur," and similar interpretations which a person is certain are not what is meant by the prohibition. Rather, the informing here is the informing of His prohibiting and obligating for Himself. The object of the report is the prohibition and the obligation, and it is not permissible to nullify the object of the report, for that would invalidate the report. This is why, when someone says: "I have obligated fasting upon myself," its object is the obligation of fasting upon himself. If it were said that it means "I informed that I fast," that would be nullifying and invalidating the purpose of the report. So reflect on this.

And since it is intelligible from a person that he obligates himself, prohibits himself, and commands and forbids himself, even though he is under the command and prohibition of another, then how can it be impossible for the One above whom there is no commander and no forbidder to prohibit for Himself and prescribe for Himself? His prescribing for Himself necessitates His will for what He has prescribed, His love for it, and His approval of it. His prohibiting for Himself necessitates His hatred of what He has prohibited, His dislike of it, and His will that it not be done. His love for the act requires its occurrence from Him, and His dislike of doing it prevents its occurrence from Him. This is different from what He loves and hates of the actions of His servants, for His love of those actions from them does not necessitate their occurrence, and His dislike of them does not prevent their occurrence. So there is a difference between His own act, glory be to Him, and the act of His servants which occurs despite His dislike and hatred of it, and which fails to occur despite His love of it and approval of it. The former is one type and the latter is another type. So contemplate this station, which is the place where the feet of the earlier and later generations slipped, except those whom God protected and guided to the straight path. And consider where His love and hatred necessitate the existence of the act and prevent its occurrence, and where love from Him and dislike do not necessitate the existence of the act nor prevent its occurrence.

The crux of the matter is the difference between what He wills to do Himself and what He does not will to do, and between what He loves from His servant that the servant do or not do.

Whoever verifies this station is freed from doubts in which groups of theologians and speculative scholars have become entangled. And God is the Guide to the right path.

Know that people in this station are of three groups. One group denied that anything could be obligatory upon Him or forbidden for Him by His own obligation and prohibition. These are many of the affirmers of divine decree (qadar), who rejected the sayings of the Qadariyya (deniers of decree) and confronted them with such strength that, because of it, they negated wisdom, causes, and rational causation, and negated that the servant be an agent or a chooser. The second group, in opposition to these, obligated things upon the Lord and prohibited things for Him by their own reason, making these into a law for Him that He must observe, without Him having obligated it upon Himself or prohibited it. They obligated upon Him things of the same kind as what is obligatory for the servants, and prohibited for Him things of the same kind as what is prohibited for them. For this reason they were anthropomorphists (Mushabbiha) in acts. The Mu'tazila among them combined two falsehoods: they negated His attributes and denied the qualities of His perfection, and they likened Him to His creation in what they obligated and prohibited upon Him. They likened Him in His acts and negated Him in the attributes of His perfection. They denied some of what He described Himself with of the attributes of perfection, and they called that monotheism (tawhid). They likened Him to His creation in what they deemed good or bad for themselves in actions, and they called that justice (‘adl). They said: "We are the people of justice and monotheism." Their justice was the denial of His power and His all-encompassing will, which excludes nothing of existing things, whether their essences, attributes, or actions. Their monotheism was their deviation regarding His beautiful names and their distortion of their meanings from what they are. So their monotheism was in reality a negation, and their justice was a form of polytheism. This is established in its proper place.

They did not obligate anything upon Him, nor prohibit anything for Him. Rather, they reported about Him what He reported about Himself, and their hearts witnessed what is within that obligation and prohibition of wisdom and praiseworthy ends, for which He deserves complete praise and commendation. The servants cannot enumerate praise of Him ever; rather He is as He praised Himself. This is clear, by God's praise, to the people of knowledge and faith. It is firmly established in their nature and fixed in their hearts.
